frontmatter.title: Self-Determination Theory: Autonomy, Competence, and Relatedness as Learning Drivers — A Focused Analysis
frontmatter.analytical-focus: How the three basic psychological needs in SDT function as learning drivers — examining the mechanistic role of need satisfaction and thwarting, the internalization spectrum from controlled to autonomous regulation, and the autonomy-supportive versus controlling distinction as the central environmental lever.

key-frameworks.name: Basic Psychological Needs Theory (BPNT)
key-frameworks.description: Sub-theory of SDT positing three universal, innate psychological needs

key-frameworks.name: Cognitive Evaluation Theory (CET)
key-frameworks.description: Sub-theory explaining how external events affect intrinsic motivation

key-frameworks.name: Organismic Integration Theory (OIT)
key-frameworks.description: Sub-theory describing the internalization and integration of extrinsic motivation
key-frameworks.validation: strong empirical base in educational contexts

frontmatter.target-audience: Educators, instructional designers, learning scientists, and practitioners with foundational background in motivational psychology who seek rigorous, mechanistic understanding of SDT in learning contexts
key-arguments: Need thwarting produces stronger and more durable negative effects on learning than need satisfaction produces positive effects — an asymmetry the mainstream SDT literature underemphasizes
The three needs are mutually constitutive rather than additive: satisfaction of one amplifies the motivational yield of the others, while thwarting one degrades the others

Autonomy support is not permissiveness but structure delivered in an autonomy-affirming manner — the conflation of these two dimensions is the primary implementation failure in educational applications of SDT
key-distinctions: Autonomy (self-endorsement of behavior) vs. Independence (absence of reliance on others)
Need Satisfaction (active fulfilment) vs. Need Deprivation (passive absence) vs. Need Thwarting (active frustration)
Internalization (taking external regulation in) vs. Integration (making it fully one's own)

expansion-topics.topic: [[Need-Thwarting-Mechanisms-and-Ill-Being-—-A-Focused-Analysis|Need Thwarting Mechanisms and Ill-Being — A Focused Analysis]]
expansion-topics.description: The asymmetry between need satisfaction and need thwarting deserves dedicated treatment — examining the specific mechanisms by which thwarting produces controlled motivation, amotivation, and psychological ill-being, and what instructional practices are most corrosive

expansion-topics.topic: [[Cultural Universality vs. Cultural Moderation in SDT]]
expansion-topics.description: SDT claims cross-cultural universality of basic needs, yet evidence reveals systematic cultural moderation of effect sizes — analyzing the universality argument, the critiques, and what genuine cross-cultural nuance looks like

expansion-topics.topic: [[Autonomy Support in Digital and AI-Mediated Learning]]
expansion-topics.description: How SDT principles apply (and require adaptation) in adaptive learning systems, AI tutors, and gamified platforms — examining the unique affordances and risks these environments present for need satisfaction

Deep analysis of the integration end of the OIT spectrum — how and why some students fully integrate academic values while others plateau at identified regulation, and what this means for long-term academic identity

expansion-topics.topic: [[SDT and Assessment: Formative Feedback as Informational vs. Controlling]]
expansion-topics.description: How different assessment practices and feedback delivery styles satisfy or thwart competence and autonomy needs — practical implications for feedback design

expansion-topics.topic: [[Comparing SDT with Achievement Goal Theory: Integration Possibilities]]
expansion-topics.description: SDT and Achievement Goal Theory (Elliot, Dweck) address overlapping terrain with different emphases — analyzing the theoretical tensions, complementarities, and whether an integrated account is possible

empirical-support: Deci et al. (1999) meta-analysis of 128 studies on rewards and intrinsic motivation
Vansteenkiste et al. (2019) systematic review of need satisfaction in educational contexts
Reeve & Jang (2006) observational study of autonomy-supportive vs. controlling teaching behaviors
Niemiec & Ryan (2009) review of SDT applications in education
Assor et al. (2002) empirical study of conditional regard and need thwarting
limitations-noted: Most intervention studies are short-term; long-term effects of sustained autonomy-supportive environments are less well-documented
The causal architecture between the three needs is difficult to untangle in field research where need satisfaction tends to co-occur

callouts.title: Prediction Point
callouts.body: Before reading further, take a moment to articulate your current intuition: Which of the three basic needs — autonomy, competence, or relatedness — do you believe is the *most* important driver of learning outcomes? Why? Is one need primary, or are they genuinely co-equal? Commit to a position. The evidence on this question is more complex and surprising than most practitioners expect, and your starting position will sharpen what you notice as you read.

callouts.title: Intrinsic Motivation
callouts.body: The tendency to engage in activities for their inherent interest and enjoyment, without requiring separable external outcomes as justification. Intrinsically motivated behavior is characterized by curiosity, spontaneous engagement, persistence in the absence of surveillance, and positive affect. Critically, intrinsic motivation is NOT the same as enjoying the outcomes of an activity — a student who studies hard to receive praise is not intrinsically motivated, even if they enjoy the praise. What distinguishes intrinsic motivation is that the activity itself is the end, not merely a means to another end.

callouts.title: Basic Psychological Needs
callouts.body: On SDT's account, basic psychological needs are innate psychological nutriments whose ongoing satisfaction is required for psychological health, growth, and the maintenance of intrinsic motivation and well-internalized extrinsic motivation. They are described as "basic" in the technical sense that their satisfaction (not merely their expression or pursuit) is hypothesized to be universally beneficial and their thwarting universally harmful — not as a matter of preference or culture but as a matter of psychological functioning. The theory identifies three: **autonomy**, **competence**, and **relatedness**.

callouts.title: Autonomy (in SDT)
callouts.body: The need to experience one's actions as self-endorsed — to feel that one is acting from one's own values and choices rather than under external pressure or internal compulsion. Autonomy in SDT does NOT mean independence, self-sufficiency, or the absence of reliance on others. A student can be fully autonomous while following a teacher's structured assignment, if they understand and genuinely endorse the reasons for that assignment. Conversely, a student choosing their own learning path under intense social pressure to succeed is not autonomous. Autonomy is about the locus of perceived causality — whether the source of behavior feels internal or external.

callouts.title: Competence (in SDT)
callouts.body: The need to experience oneself as effective in interaction with the environment — to feel capable, to master challenges, and to bring about desired outcomes. Competence in SDT is not an objective measure of ability but a psychological experience of effectance. This experience is sustained when challenges are optimally calibrated (sufficiently challenging to require effort, but achievable with effort), when feedback is informational and positive, and when progress is visible. Environments that are either too easy (no growth) or too difficult (repeated failure without scaffolding) undermine the competence need.

callouts.title: Relatedness (in SDT)
callouts.body: The need to feel securely connected to others, to experience care and belonging, and to feel that one matters to the people around them. Relatedness in SDT does not require close friendship or intimacy — it can be satisfied by a classroom culture where students feel respected and valued by their teacher and peers. The critical functional requirement is felt security: that one's standing in the relational environment is not contingent on performance.

callouts.title: The Mutual Amplification Hypothesis
callouts.body: The three needs are not independent silos. Satisfaction of one need tends to amplify the motivational yield of the others, while thwarting of one degrades the others' functioning. A student who feels autonomously engaged in a task is more able to experience competence-relevant feedback as informational rather than threatening. A student who feels related — cared for and secure — is better positioned to take the risks that competence development requires. Treating the needs as additive components misses the dynamic interdependence that field research increasingly confirms.

callouts.title: The Regulatory Spectrum (OIT)
callouts.body:
OIT proposes six regulatory styles arranged from least to most autonomous:

1. **Amotivation** — absence of intentional regulation; the person does not act or acts without intention
2. **External Regulation** — behavior controlled by external rewards and punishments; fully controlled regulation
3. **Introjected Regulation** — regulation by internalized pressures: ego-involvement, guilt, shame, contingent self-worth; still controlled, but the controlling force is now internal
4. **Identified Regulation** — the person consciously values the goal and acts from that valuation; autonomous, though not yet integrated with broader self
5. **Integrated Regulation** — the identified goal has been integrated with the person's core values and identity; fully autonomous and extrinsic
6. **Intrinsic Motivation** — behavior performed for its inherent interest; fully autonomous and inherently rewarding

callouts.title: Conceptual Checkpoint
callouts.body: The analysis ahead depends entirely on the distinction between *controlled* and *autonomous* regulation — and, critically, on the distinction between *autonomous* and *intrinsic* regulation. Before proceeding: Can you explain, in your own words, why a student who studies because they genuinely value learning (identified regulation) is motivationally more similar to a student who loves the subject (intrinsic motivation) than to a student who studies to avoid parental disapproval (introjected regulation), even though the first two cases both involve external content? If you find yourself uncertain, re-read the regulatory spectrum definition — the entire Phase IV analysis depends on this distinction.

callouts.title: Autonomy-Supportive Environment
callouts.body: An environment that takes the perspective of the learner, acknowledges and works with the learner's feelings and perspective (even when those feelings involve resistance or disinterest), provides meaningful rationale for requirements, uses informational rather than controlling language, and minimizes external pressure while nurturing internal motivational resources. Autonomy support is NOT the absence of structure, expectations, or guidance. It is the way structure and guidance are delivered — with acknowledgment of the learner's perspective and genuine respect for their agency.

callouts.title: Controlling Environment
callouts.body: An environment that pressures learners toward specific outcomes through rewards, punishments, surveillance, deadlines presented as sources of pressure, praise that is evaluative rather than informational, conditional regard (where teacher warmth is contingent on performance), and language that communicates "you must," "you should," or "I will reward/punish you for." Controlling environments may produce compliance, but the compliance comes at the cost of autonomous motivation, deeper processing, and wellbeing.

callouts.title: The Autonomy-Structure Conflation: The Most Costly Error in SDT's Educational Uptake
callouts.body: The single most common implementation failure when educators learn about SDT is the equation of autonomy support with reduced structure, loose expectations, or student-directed free choice. This conflation is not only theoretically wrong — it is practically harmful. SDT's research strongly supports the importance of **structure** (clear expectations, scaffolded challenges, organized support) as a distinct and necessary dimension of need-supportive teaching. The theoretical claim is not that structure undermines autonomy, but that *how* structure is delivered — with or without acknowledgment of the learner's perspective and choice — determines whether it satisfies or thwarts the autonomy need. A highly structured, demanding learning environment can be deeply autonomy-supportive if the learner understands and endorses the reasons for the demands. A loosely structured, permissive environment can still thwart autonomy if the student feels directionless, incompetent, or relationally disconnected.

callouts.title: Integrating the Framework
callouts.body:
**Comprehension**: Explain the difference between autonomy and independence in SDT's terms. Why does this distinction matter for how we evaluate a classroom where students have "choice" in their assignments?

**Application**: Think of a learning environment you are familiar with — your own education, a workplace training, a digital learning platform. Where on the autonomous/controlled regulatory spectrum would most learners in that environment likely fall, and why? What environmental features drove your assessment?

**Extension**: SDT's regulatory spectrum is typically presented as a developmental sequence — internalization progresses from external toward integrated. But is progression always linear? Can you think of conditions under which a learner who achieved identified regulation might slide back toward introjected or external regulation? What would this imply for instructional design?

callouts.title: Knowledge State — Before
callouts.body: Before engaging with the evidence, record your current estimate: What is the magnitude of the effect of autonomy-supportive teaching on learning outcomes (achievement, persistence, depth of processing, wellbeing)? Is it a strong effect (d > 0.5), a moderate effect (d = 0.2–0.5), or a weak-but-consistent effect (d < 0.2)? And where do you expect the evidence to be strongest — on achievement outcomes, on persistence, or on wellbeing? Write this down; the comparison will be revealing.

callouts.title: Deci et al. (1999) Meta-Analysis on Rewards and Intrinsic Motivation
callouts.body: This landmark meta-analysis examined 128 studies and found that tangible, expected, and contingent rewards significantly undermine intrinsic motivation (d ≈ −0.68 for engagement, −0.61 for intrinsic motivation measures), while verbal rewards under certain conditions can enhance intrinsic motivation when delivered as genuine positive informational feedback about competence rather than as evaluation or control. The conditions under which reward effects are positive, negative, or neutral depend almost entirely on the functional significance of the reward: whether it communicates information about competence (informational function) or communicates external control (controlling function).

callouts.title: The Asymmetry of Need Satisfaction and Need Thwarting
callouts.body: The evidence, taken carefully, points toward an asymmetry that SDT's original formulations underemphasized: need thwarting produces stronger and more persistent negative outcomes than need satisfaction produces positive outcomes. Studies using need frustration scales alongside need satisfaction scales — a methodological innovation introduced by Bartholomew, Ntoumanis, and colleagues in sport contexts and extended to education by Vansteenkiste and Soenens — consistently find that need frustration is a stronger and more unique predictor of ill-being, controlled motivation, and amotivation than need satisfaction is of well-being and autonomous motivation. This asymmetry parallels findings from the positive psychology literature on the greater weight of negative affect relative to positive affect in wellbeing outcomes, and has important implications for prioritization: preventing thwarting may matter more than maximizing satisfaction.

callouts.title: Jang (2008) Experimental Study on Rationale and Internalization
callouts.body: In a carefully designed experiment, Jang provided high school students with an uninteresting grammar activity under one of three conditions: no rationale, a controlling rationale ("you need to do this because it's in the curriculum"), or an autonomy-supportive rationale (acknowledging the activity's boring nature while providing genuine, informative reasons for its value). Students in the autonomy-supportive rationale condition showed significantly higher identified regulation, persistence, and learning performance than both other conditions — demonstrating that autonomous regulation of extrinsic tasks is achievable and that instructional delivery is the critical moderator.

callouts.title: The Positive Feedback Paradox
callouts.body: CET's predictions about feedback create a genuine tension that the empirical literature has not fully resolved. The theory predicts that positive feedback is motivationally enhancing when perceived as informational, but research on ego-involvement (Nicholls, 1984) and performance goal orientation (Dweck) suggests that some students — particularly those with fragile, contingent self-esteem — process positive feedback as ego-relevant rather than task-relevant, regardless of how it is delivered. The question of whether delivery can consistently override a student's pre-existing ego-involvement mode, or whether certain learners are so entrenched in ego-involvement that autonomy-supportive feedback simply doesn't reach them, is not resolved. Effective SDT applications need to engage with individual differences in ego-involvement rather than treating feedback effects as uniformly determined by delivery style.

callouts.title: What the Evidence Suggests About Relatedness: A More Nuanced Reading
callouts.body: The evidence suggests that relatedness functions primarily as an enabling condition rather than a direct driver of specific learning behaviors. When felt security is absent — when students experience conditional regard (teacher warmth contingent on performance), when they feel socially excluded, or when peer relationships are competitive and comparison-based — the autonomy and competence needs become harder to satisfy because the learner's attentional and motivational resources are partially consumed by social threat monitoring. In high-relatedness classrooms, not only is motivation higher on average, but the *variance* in motivation is lower: fewer students are operating from fear, ego-defense, or social anxiety. The implication is that relatedness is most important as a risk-mitigation variable — its absence is more damaging than its presence is enhancing.

callouts.title: Prediction Check
callouts.body: Return to your prediction about effect sizes and outcome domains. Were you in the right range? Did you anticipate the differential effects on conceptual understanding versus rote performance? And did you predict the asymmetry between need thwarting and need satisfaction? If any of these surprised you, examine the underlying assumptions that drove your original prediction — those assumptions likely reveal important things about your current mental model of motivation.

callouts.title: Integrating the Evidence
callouts.body:
**Comprehension**: What is the single most important finding in this section, and why does it matter for the central question of how needs drive learning?

**Application**: If you were to use the need thwarting / need satisfaction distinction in your own practice or context, what specific instructional or environmental features would you examine first as potential sources of thwarting (rather than merely deprivation)?

**Extension**: The evidence for relatedness effects is described as "less well-specified" than for autonomy and competence. Design a study (in your mind) that would help clarify the direct versus mediated effects of relatedness on learning outcomes. What would you control, measure, and compare?

callouts.title: Complexity Transition
callouts.body: The analysis ahead goes deeper into mechanism and causation. It builds directly on the framework from Phase II (the three needs, the regulatory spectrum, the autonomy-support distinction) and the evidence patterns from Phase III. If those feel solid, the mechanisms ahead will substantially enrich your understanding. If any element of the regulatory spectrum — particularly the distinction between controlled and autonomous regulation, or between need thwarting and need deprivation — feels uncertain, a brief return to Phase II will pay significant dividends here.

callouts.title: The Hidden Cost of Surveillance in Learning
callouts.body: One of the most practically significant mechanisms in SDT is the effect of surveillance on PLOC and learning quality. Studies by Deci and colleagues show that even passive surveillance — simply being observed — shifts PLOC toward external, reduces intrinsic motivation, and degrades performance on subsequent free-choice activities. This has a disturbing implication for digitally-mediated learning environments that track every mouse click, keystroke, and time-on-task: the monitoring infrastructure itself may be costing some of the motivational quality it is designed to measure. This is not an argument against all monitoring, but a call for careful distinction between monitoring that communicates control (you are being watched, you must perform) and monitoring that communicates support (data is available to help you learn more effectively). The functional significance of monitoring — whether learners interpret it as surveillance or as support — is what determines its motivational impact.

callouts.title: Optimal Challenge: SDT's Competence Mechanism and the Biology of Learning
callouts.body: The SDT competence mechanism parallels what neuroscience describes as dopaminergic reward prediction error signaling. When a learner successfully handles a challenge that was at the edge of their capability, the brain registers a positive prediction error — the outcome was better than expected — and releases dopamine, strengthening the neural pathways associated with the behavior and creating a motivational pull toward similar challenges. Below-optimal challenge produces no prediction error signal (outcomes match or fall below expectations), while above-optimal challenge produces negative prediction error (repeated failure). SDT's behavioral claim that intrinsic motivation is maximized at optimal challenge is thus not merely a psychological observation — it reflects underlying neural architecture. This connection suggests that autonomy-supportive environments may be most effective precisely because they protect the learner's access to optimal challenge: when learners have some agency over task selection, they tend to self-regulate toward the challenge frontier, while controlled environments often impose challenges that are either too uniform or optimized for the average rather than the individual.

callouts.title: Competence Feedback and the Mastery-Performance Distinction
callouts.body: A subtle but important consequence of the CET competence mechanism is that it predicts a systematic interaction between regulatory style and feedback type. Learners operating from controlled regulation tend to process all feedback through a performance frame — they want to know how they compare to others or how they are being evaluated. These learners are particularly susceptible to the controlling function of feedback, because their PLOC is already external and performance-oriented. Learners operating from autonomous regulation process feedback through a mastery frame — they want to know what it tells them about what to do next. For these learners, even evaluative feedback is more likely to be processed informationally. This interaction has a practical implication that is rarely acknowledged in SDT-informed instructional design: autonomy-supportive feedback is most powerful when combined with efforts to shift learners from performance to mastery framing — which requires, in turn, addressing the competence and autonomy needs together, not separately.

callouts.title: Relatedness as Risk Architecture
callouts.body: Learning requires risk: asking a question that might reveal ignorance, attempting a difficult problem that might result in failure, offering an original idea that might be criticized, admitting confusion in a context where others may judge you for it. The willingness to take these risks is not a fixed personality trait — it is a dynamic function of the learner's felt security in the relational environment. When relatedness is well-satisfied, the learner's psychological resources are available for risk-taking because failure does not threaten their standing in the community. When relatedness is thwarted — through conditional regard, social comparison, exclusion, or indifference — the learner's resources are partially consumed by social threat monitoring, and the risk budget for intellectual engagement shrinks accordingly. This is why the "psychological safety" construct in organizational research (Edmondson, 1999) maps so closely onto SDT's relatedness need: psychological safety is essentially the organizational-context version of relatedness satisfaction.

callouts.title: The Universality Claim and Cultural Moderation
callouts.body: SDT asserts that the three basic needs are universal — that their satisfaction is beneficial and their thwarting harmful across all human beings regardless of cultural background. This universality claim has generated substantial debate, particularly in cross-cultural psychology. Research in East Asian educational contexts has sometimes found weaker (though rarely reversed) effects of autonomy support on motivation, and evidence from collectivist cultures suggests that relatedness may, in some contexts, function as a more powerful regulatory mechanism than autonomy — meaning that social belonging and conformity to in-group norms can partially substitute for autonomous regulation in maintaining academic engagement. SDT's proponents respond that the universality claim is not that need satisfaction always looks the same across cultures, but that the functional relationships hold universally: autonomy satisfaction always predicts better outcomes than autonomy thwarting, even if the behaviors that constitute "autonomy support" vary across cultural contexts. The tension is not fully resolved, and practitioners working in diverse cultural contexts should treat the universality claim with appropriate nuance rather than as a license to export Western autonomy-support frameworks without adaptation.

callouts.title: The Paradox of Scaffolding Without Autonomy Support
callouts.body: A particularly important implication of the needs' interaction involves the limits of scaffolding. Scaffolding — carefully structured support that reduces task complexity to the learner's current level and gradually withdraws — is a powerful pedagogical tool for satisfying the competence need. But in controlling instructional climates, scaffolding can paradoxically undermine motivation by communicating low confidence in the learner's capabilities, shifting PLOC toward the external (the structure is doing it, not me), and producing competence attributions ("I succeeded because the task was easy") rather than efficacy attributions ("I succeeded because I can do this"). The scaffold itself, if not delivered in an autonomy-supportive manner, can become a source of controlled regulation. This suggests that the motivational value of scaffolding depends critically on how it is framed: as "I'm giving you this support because you can't do this yet" versus "I'm giving you this support so you can experience success at the frontier of your current ability."

callouts.title: Calibration Check
callouts.body: Rate your current understanding of the mechanisms in this section on a scale of 1–10. Now, without looking back, try to explain: (1) Why does surveillance reduce learning quality, mechanistically? (2) What is the "risk budget" role of relatedness, and how does conditional regard undermine it? (3) How does the autonomy-competence positive feedback loop break down in controlling environments? Compare your performance to your confidence rating. Any gap between them — in either direction — is valuable metacognitive information.

callouts.title: Integrating the Mechanisms
callouts.body:
**Comprehension**: Which mechanism — autonomy's PLOC effect, competence's optimal challenge dependency, or relatedness's risk architecture — changed your understanding the most? Trace the causal chain for that mechanism from environmental input to learning outcome.

**Application**: Think of a specific instructional design decision you make or observe (a deadline, a grading rubric, a discussion prompt, a feedback format). Which need does it most directly address? Which mechanism is it engaging? Could it be redesigned to engage that mechanism more cleanly?

**Extension**: Consider a situation where satisfying one need might temporarily undermine another. For instance: a teacher provides very positive, enthusiastic feedback to motivate a struggling student (satisfying relatedness). Under what conditions might this undermine competence satisfaction or shift PLOC in the wrong direction?

callouts.title: Prioritize Need-Thwarting Prevention Over Need-Satisfaction Maximization
callouts.body: Given the evidence asymmetry between need thwarting and need satisfaction, the most impactful instructional decisions are those that *eliminate* active frustration of needs, not merely those that *add* need-satisfying elements. An autonomy-supportive feedback system sitting atop a classroom culture of conditional regard, social comparison, and surveillance is likely to produce minimal motivational yield. Audit for thwarting before adding satisfaction.

callouts.title: Design for Optimal Challenge at the Individual Level, Not the Average
callouts.body: The competence mechanism requires individualized challenge calibration. Uniform assessments, single-path curricula, and whole-class pacing undermine competence experience for both above-average and below-average learners simultaneously. The practical implication is not that every student needs a unique curriculum, but that enough variability and choice must be built into the learning environment to allow students to operate near their own challenge frontier.

callouts.title: Deliver Structure Autonomy-Supportively
callouts.body: The most actionable single change available to most instructors is the delivery mode of structure, not the amount of structure. The same requirement, the same deadline, the same standard can be delivered in ways that acknowledge the learner's perspective (autonomy-supportive structure) or that simply impose the requirement (controlling structure). The critical elements: acknowledging that the requirement may feel burdensome, providing genuine rationale, and communicating genuine interest in the learner's perspective on it.

callouts.title: Misconception: Rewards Always Undermine Motivation
callouts.body: The popular appropriation of SDT's evidence on rewards frequently overgeneralizes to "rewards are bad." The actual claim is more nuanced: rewards undermine intrinsic motivation when they shift PLOC toward external, communicate control, and signal that the task is instrumental rather than valuable in itself. Unexpected rewards, verbal praise delivered informationally, and task-noncontingent rewards (given for participation rather than performance) do not carry these properties and do not show consistent demotivating effects. The practical guidance is not to eliminate rewards but to examine their functional significance: what does this reward communicate to the learner about who controls their engagement with this material?

callouts.title: Misconception: Autonomy Support Means Student Choice
callouts.body: As noted in Phase II, autonomy support is not the same as giving students choices about what to do. Autonomous regulation can be achieved in highly structured, teacher-directed environments if the learner genuinely understands and endorses the reasons for the direction. Conversely, environments offering extensive choice can still produce controlled regulation if choices are presented in ways that highlight performance consequences or social comparison. The locus of causality — not the structural source of the task — is what matters.

callouts.title: Limitation: The Causal Identification Problem
callouts.body: Most field evidence for SDT in education is correlational or quasi-experimental. Because autonomy, competence, and relatedness satisfaction tend to co-occur in good teaching relationships, and because good teaching tends to also involve better content, clearer explanations, and higher student ability — all confounded with need satisfaction — causal attribution is difficult. The experimental evidence (manipulating individual need satisfaction while holding others constant) is cleaner but more artificial. The practical guidance from SDT is well-grounded, but practitioners should maintain appropriate epistemic humility about which specific need is driving which specific outcome in any particular setting.

callouts.title: Limitation: Long-Term Effects and Ecological Validity
callouts.body: The majority of SDT intervention studies in education are short-term — weeks to a semester, rarely longer. Whether the motivational benefits of sustained autonomy-supportive environments compound over years of schooling, or whether effects plateau, is less well-documented. Longitudinal work by Vansteenkiste and colleagues offers encouraging evidence of cumulative effects, but this literature is younger and more methodologically varied.

callouts.title: Limitation: Cultural and Individual Boundary Conditions
callouts.body: As flagged in Phase IV, the universality claim requires cultural sensitivity in application. Additionally, SDT research has devoted less attention to individual differences in need strength and need prominence. Some learners may show higher sensitivity to competence thwarting than to autonomy thwarting, or vice versa — clinical populations, learners with anxiety disorders, and learners with histories of academic trauma may respond to need-support interventions quite differently than the population averages suggest.

callouts.title: Knowledge State — After
callouts.body: Return to what you recorded before Phase III. How has your position on the central question — how the three needs function as learning drivers — shifted? Was the shift primarily additive (you now know more mechanisms) or transformative (the underlying framework changed)? Which of the evidence findings most significantly updated your prior beliefs? And what remains genuinely uncertain for you?

callouts.title: Integrating the Implications
callouts.body:
**Comprehension**: What is the most important limitation of this analysis, and how does it affect your confidence in the recommendations?

**Application**: If you were implementing one insight from this report in your own practice this week, which would it be, and what specific behavior would change?

**Extension**: The analysis recommends "audit for thwarting before adding satisfaction." What would such an audit look like in practice? What specific behaviors, structures, or language patterns would you examine as potential sources of need thwarting?

callouts.title: The Integrated Gateway Model: Autonomy as the Motivational Gatekeeper
callouts.body: Bringing the three need mechanisms together, I propose that the relationship among the needs is not symmetric but hierarchical in a specific functional sense: *autonomy satisfaction acts as a motivational gateway that determines whether competence and relatedness experiences can be fully processed as need-satisfying*. When autonomy is thwarted and PLOC is external, the learner processes competence feedback through a performance frame (ego-threat rather than information) and processes relational experiences through a social monitoring frame (status management rather than security). This is why controlling environments produce such broad motivational damage even when they provide rich competence scaffolding and warm teacher relationships: the scaffolding becomes a reminder of dependence, and the warmth becomes conditional regard in perception. Conversely, when autonomy is genuinely supported, competence and relatedness experiences become fully available as motivational fuel. The practical implication is that autonomy-support is not one of three equally important needs to satisfy — it is the prerequisite condition under which satisfying the other two needs becomes motivationally possible. Structure, scaffolding, and relational warmth are necessary but not sufficient; they must be delivered in an autonomy-affirming manner to achieve their full motivational yield.

callouts.title: Need Satisfaction as Dynamic Equilibrium, Not Cumulative Score
callouts.body: A second synthetic insight: it is tempting to treat need satisfaction as a kind of psychological bank account — make enough deposits (autonomy-supportive moments, competence-building experiences, warm relational interactions) and the account balance grows, supporting motivation long-term. The evidence suggests a different model. Need satisfaction is more like a dynamic equilibrium than a cumulative score: it must be continuously maintained, because the effects of thwarting are rapid and can quickly override a history of satisfaction. A classroom that has been reliably autonomy-supportive for months can generate acute thwarting damage within a single high-stakes, controlling assessment event. The practical implication is that need support is not something to achieve and sustain in a background sense — it is an ongoing dynamic that requires attention in each instructional interaction, especially during the high-stakes moments that are most tempting to deliver in controlling rather than autonomy-supportive ways.

callouts.title: Final Integration
callouts.body:
**Comprehension**: What is the single most important analytical contribution of this report — the insight that most changes how you think about SDT as a learning driver?

**Application**: Explain the core argument of this analysis to a colleague in three sentences, focusing on what is different from the standard SDT account they might already know.

**Extension**: The gateway model proposed here — autonomy as motivational gatekeeper — makes a testable prediction: interventions that improve autonomy support should produce larger effects on learning outcomes than competence-only or relatedness-only interventions, even controlling for the amount of need satisfaction provided. How would you design a study to test this prediction rigorously?

callouts.title: Untitled
callouts.body:
**Internal PKB Connections:**

This focused analysis of SDT as a learning driver connects substantively to several adjacent areas in your knowledge base:

- **[[Growth-Mindset-and-Incremental-Intelligence-Theory|Growth Mindset and Incremental Intelligence Theory]]** — Dweck's growth mindset research and SDT's competence mechanism are deeply complementary but often treated separately. Both identify the challenge-seeking orientation as foundational to learning motivation; growth mindset addresses *beliefs about intelligence* as a moderator, while SDT's competence mechanism addresses *environmental conditions* as determinants. The interaction is theoretically important: a learner with a strong growth mindset may be better able to preserve autonomous competence-seeking even in mildly controlling environments, while a learner with a fixed mindset may be especially vulnerable to competence thwarting because failure confirms a fixed-ability narrative. Understanding this interaction requires integrating both frameworks.

- **[[Metacognition-and-Self-Regulated-Learning|Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning]]** — Self-regulated learning (SRL) and SDT address motivation from different angles. SRL frameworks (Zimmerman, Pintrich) describe the cognitive-metacognitive processes learners deploy to manage their learning; SDT describes the motivational conditions under which those processes are deployed with full engagement versus defensiveness or disengagement. The connection is that autonomous regulation is essentially the motivational precondition for self-regulation: learners can only engage in genuine self-monitoring, self-evaluation, and adaptive strategy deployment when they are motivated by mastery rather than performance management. SRL without SDT-compatible environments produces self-regulation in service of controlled goals.

- **[[Psychological-Safety-in-Learning-Environments|Psychological Safety in Learning Environments]]** — Edmondson's psychological safety construct (developed in organizational contexts) maps directly onto SDT's relatedness mechanism and risk architecture analysis. Both frameworks converge on the same functional claim: when felt relational safety is absent, risk-taking (intellectual, creative, experimental) is suppressed. Cross-referencing these two literatures strengthens both: SDT provides the needs-based theoretical mechanism for why psychological safety matters, while the organizational literature provides implementation-level evidence about how team leaders and teachers can create safety through specific behaviors (listening, non-judgment, welcoming error as information).

- **[[Expectancy-Value-Theory|Expectancy-Value Theory]]** — Wigfield and Eccles' expectancy-value theory addresses motivation through learners' expectations of success and subjective task value. SDT and EVT are complementary in identifying why task value matters: in SDT terms, perceiving a task as valuable is the cognitive marker of identified regulation — the student has cognitively connected the task to their own goals and values. SDT goes further by identifying the *environmental conditions* that promote this value integration (autonomy support, rationale provision), while EVT goes further in specifying the content of subjective value (utility, interest, attainment, cost). Together they provide a fuller picture of academic motivation than either alone.

- **[[Gamification-in-Learning|Gamification in Learning]]** — Gamification is a theoretically interesting application domain for SDT because game mechanics can easily thwart or satisfy the three needs depending on implementation. Points, leaderboards, and badges are classic reward structures that CET predicts will undermine intrinsic motivation when they shift PLOC toward external — and the evidence from gamification research is consistent with this: competition-based leaderboards tend to undermine motivation for below-average performers and produce performance-goal orientation for all. Game mechanics that satisfy the competence need (optimal challenge, immediate feedback, mastery-based progression) and the autonomy need (choice, meaningful decisions, narrative agency) are more consistent with SDT's predictions about long-term engagement. This tension between popular gamification practice and SDT principles is a productive site for both research and design innovation.

**Cross-Report Links:**

- **[[Self-Determination-Theory-—-Foundational-Overview|Self-Determination Theory — Foundational Overview]]** — This analysis extends the foundational treatment by drilling into the specific mechanisms through which each need drives learning outcomes, adding the need thwarting / need satisfaction asymmetry analysis, and offering the gateway model as an original synthesis. Readers should consult the foundational report for historical development, sub-theory architecture, and broad empirical landscape before engaging with this analysis.

**Synthetic Observation:** The pattern of connections visible in this knowledge graph reveals that SDT occupies a distinctive theoretical position: it provides the *motivational mechanism layer* that many other frameworks in learning science presuppose without explaining. Growth mindset theory tells us what beliefs matter; SDT explains what environmental conditions produce those beliefs. SRL theory tells us what processes matter; SDT explains what motivational conditions make those processes available. Psychological safety research tells us what relational conditions matter; SDT explains *why* they matter through the relatedness mechanism. SDT is less a standalone framework than an explanatory infrastructure that makes other learning frameworks motivationally intelligible.

callouts.title: Amotivation
callouts.body: The absence of intentional regulation — the state in which a person either does not engage in a behavior at all, or engages without any intention behind the action. In learning contexts, amotivation is typically the result of sustained need thwarting: the learner has given up any sense that engagement will satisfy their needs. Distinguished from disinterest (which can coexist with intrinsic motivation for other topics) by its global quality and its association with helplessness, passivity, and disengagement from academic life broadly.

callouts.title: Autonomous Regulation
callouts.body: The umbrella category in OIT encompassing identified regulation, integrated regulation, and intrinsic motivation — all forms of motivation in which the learner experiences the source of their engagement as arising from their own values and choices. Autonomous regulation is associated with deeper processing, greater persistence, higher wellbeing, and more positive academic emotions. The key functional marker is an internal perceived locus of causality.

callouts.title: Cognitive Evaluation Theory (CET)
callouts.body: SDT's sub-theory addressing the effects of external events (rewards, feedback, deadlines, surveillance) on intrinsic motivation. CET proposes that any external event carries both an informational aspect (conveying something about competence) and a controlling aspect (conveying something about who is determining behavior). The relative salience of these two aspects determines whether the external event enhances (informational dominant) or undermines (controlling dominant) intrinsic motivation.

callouts.title: Conditional Regard
callouts.body: Teacher or parent warmth that is contingent on student performance or compliance — love and approval are available when the student succeeds but withheld when the student fails or resists. A documented form of relatedness thwarting that produces introjected regulation (students internalize the contingency — "I am valuable when I perform") rather than identified or integrated regulation. Associated with high anxiety, fragile self-esteem, and vulnerability to collapse of motivation under failure conditions.

callouts.title: Controlled Regulation
callouts.body: The umbrella category in OIT encompassing external and introjected regulation — all forms of motivation in which the learner experiences the source of their engagement as external pressure or internal compulsion (guilt, shame, ego-threat). Controlled regulation is associated with surface processing, performance orientation, higher anxiety, and reduced wellbeing. The functional marker is an external or impersonal perceived locus of causality.

callouts.title: Effectance
callouts.body: The subjective experience of being effective in interaction with the environment — the psychological state of genuine competence satisfaction. Effectance is not the same as objective performance: a student can perform well without experiencing effectance (if success feels attributable to luck, scaffolding, or low task difficulty) and can experience effectance from failure in the right challenge context (when effort was appropriate and feedback is informational). The SDT competence need is for effectance experience, not for objective achievement.

callouts.title: Identified Regulation
callouts.body: The regulatory style in which the learner consciously values the goal and engages with the activity because they judge it personally important, even if it is not intrinsically interesting. Identified regulation is classified as autonomous because the source of regulation is the learner's own evaluative judgment. A student who studies for a required course because they genuinely see its value for their goals — even if they find the specific material dry — is exhibiting identified regulation.

callouts.title: Introjected Regulation
callouts.body: The regulatory style in which the learner is driven by internalized pressures: guilt, shame, ego-threat, or the need to maintain contingent self-esteem. Introjected regulation is classified as controlled even though the source of pressure is internal, because the learner is not freely choosing engagement — they are responding to internal compulsions that feel obligatory rather than chosen. Students who study primarily to avoid feeling like a failure are exhibiting introjected regulation.

callouts.title: Need Thwarting (vs. Need Deprivation)
callouts.body: Need thwarting refers to the *active frustration* of a psychological need — instructional behaviors, social conditions, or environmental features that specifically undermine need satisfaction. Distinguished from need deprivation (the passive absence of need satisfaction) by its causal specificity and its stronger association with ill-being, controlled motivation, and amotivation. Thwarting can occur even when overall need satisfaction is moderate, and its effects are not simply the mirror image of satisfaction effects.

callouts.title: Organismic Integration Theory (OIT)
callouts.body: The SDT sub-theory addressing the internalization and integration of extrinsic motivation — the process by which externally-imposed regulations can be progressively taken in and made one's own. OIT proposes the regulatory spectrum as a model of internalization progress, and identifies autonomy support, competence scaffolding, and relational security as the conditions that facilitate movement toward more autonomous regulatory styles.

callouts.title: Perceived Locus of Causality (PLOC)
callouts.body: The learner's subjective experience of the origin of their behavior — whether they feel that their engagement arises from their own choices and values (internal PLOC) or from external demands and pressures (external PLOC). PLOC is the central mechanism through which autonomy support affects motivational quality: autonomy-supportive environments shift PLOC toward internal, while controlling environments shift it toward external.

callouts.title: Deci, E. L., & Ryan, R. M. (1985). *Intrinsic Motivation and Self-Determination in Human Behavior*. Plenum.
callouts.body: The foundational theoretical work establishing SDT's original architecture, including Cognitive Evaluation Theory and the initial formulation of Organismic Integration Theory. Essential for understanding the theory's philosophical commitments (organismic, dialectical) and its historical grounding in experimental research on rewards and intrinsic motivation. Sections 3–5 are most directly relevant to educational applications.

callouts.title: Deci, E. L., Koestner, R., & Ryan, R. M. (1999). A meta-analytic review of experiments examining the effects of extrinsic rewards on intrinsic motivation. *Psychological Bulletin, 126*(6), 627–668.
callouts.body: The most comprehensive empirical review of the reward-undermining-motivation literature, synthesizing 128 experimental studies. Critical for understanding the conditional nature of reward effects and for correcting the popular overgeneralization that "all rewards are harmful." Table 3 provides a useful breakdown of reward type by effect direction.

callouts.title: Ryan, R. M., & Deci, E. L. (2000). Self-determination theory and the facilitation of intrinsic motivation, social development, and well-being. *American Psychologist, 55*(1), 68–78.
callouts.body: The key programmatic statement of modern SDT, introducing Basic Psychological Needs Theory as a formal sub-theory and articulating the three-need framework with clear psychological definitions. Widely cited as the entry point for the modern SDT literature; supports Phases II and III of this analysis.

callouts.title: Jang, H. (2008). Supporting students' motivation, engagement, and learning during an uninteresting activity. *Journal of Educational Psychology, 100*(4), 798–811.
callouts.body: Experimental study providing clean evidence for the role of rationale in promoting internalization of extrinsic motivation. The design elegantly isolates delivery mode from task content, making it one of the clearest demonstrations of the autonomy-support mechanism. Cited in Phase III's treatment of internalization evidence.

callouts.title: Vansteenkiste, M., & Ryan, R. M. (2013). On psychological growth and vulnerability: Basic psychological need satisfaction and need frustration as a unifying principle. *Journal of Psychotherapy Integration, 23*(3), 263–280.
callouts.body: The theoretical paper most directly addressing the need thwarting / need deprivation distinction and the asymmetry between satisfaction and thwarting effects. Foundational for the Phase III evidence review and the Phase V practical recommendations.

callouts.title: Reeve, J., & Jang, H. (2006). What teachers say and do to support students' autonomy during a learning activity. *Journal of Educational Psychology, 98*(1), 209–218.
callouts.body: Observational coding study identifying specific teacher behaviors associated with autonomy support and control. Provides empirical grounding for the behavioral catalogue of autonomy-supportive teaching. Useful as a practical reference for the behaviors described in Phase V.

callouts.title: Assor, A., Roth, G., & Deci, E. L. (2004). The emotional costs of parents' conditional regard: A self-determination theory analysis. *Journal of Personality, 72*(1), 47–88.
callouts.body: Empirical study examining conditional regard as a form of relatedness thwarting and its association with introjected regulation, contingent self-esteem, and fragile academic motivation. Supports the Phase IV analysis of conditional regard and the relatedness risk-architecture mechanism.

callouts.title: Niemiec, C. P., & Ryan, R. M. (2009). Autonomy, competence, and relatedness in the classroom: Applying self-determination theory to educational practice. *Theory and Research in Education, 7*(2), 133–144.
callouts.body: A practitioner-oriented review of SDT evidence in educational contexts, synthesizing the empirical literature into guidelines for classroom application. Useful as a supplement to this analysis for readers seeking a broader survey of the educational SDT literature.

callouts.title: Bartholomew, K. J., Ntoumanis, N., Ryan, R. M., Bosch, J. A., & Thøgersen-Ntoumani, C. (2011). Self-determination theory and diminished functioning: The role of interpersonal control and psychological need thwarting. *Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 37*(11), 1459–1473.
callouts.body: Methodologically important paper introducing the distinction between need satisfaction and need frustration scales, demonstrating that need frustration is a distinct and uniquely predictive construct rather than simply the low end of a satisfaction continuum. Essential empirical grounding for the asymmetry claim in Phase III.

callouts.title: Vansteenkiste, M., Sierens, E., Goossens, L., Soenens, B., Dochy, F., Mouratidis, A., ... & Beyers, W. (2012). Identifying configurations of perceived teacher autonomy support and structure: Associations with self-regulated learning, motivation and problem behavior. *Learning and Instruction, 22*(6), 431–439.
callouts.body: Empirical study examining the interaction between autonomy support and structure in educational contexts, providing evidence that the combination of both — rather than either alone — produces the strongest motivational and learning outcomes. Directly relevant to the Phase II and Phase V discussions of the autonomy-structure distinction.

callouts.title: Research Grounding for This Report
callouts.body:
This analysis draws on approximately five decades of SDT research, with heaviest reliance on meta-analytic syntheses, experimental studies, and theory-development papers from Deci, Ryan, Vansteenkiste, Reeve, Assor, and colleagues. The empirical claims in Phases III and IV are grounded in this literature and represent well-established findings within the SDT tradition.

The following distinctions apply across the analysis: (1) **Empirically established claims** include the reward-undermining-intrinsic-motivation effect, the learning advantages of autonomous over controlled regulation, and the internalization effect of autonomy-supportive rationale provision — all supported by multiple experimental studies and meta-analyses. (2) **Theoretically grounded integrations** include the mutual amplification account and the risk-architecture framing of relatedness — well-supported by convergent empirical evidence but not tested as unified constructs in single studies. (3) **Claude's original analytical contributions** include the Gateway Model (autonomy as motivational gatekeeper for the other two needs) and the Dynamic Equilibrium Model (need satisfaction as ongoing maintenance rather than cumulative score) — presented as theoretically motivated syntheses consistent with the evidence but not directly tested as stated. These contributions represent analytical extensions of the SDT framework, not established theoretical claims.

callouts.title: [[Need-Thwarting-Mechanisms-and-Ill-Being-—-A-Focused-Analysis|Need Thwarting Mechanisms and Ill-Being — A Focused Analysis]]
callouts.body: This analysis repeatedly flagged the need thwarting / need deprivation asymmetry as one of the most theoretically significant and practically underappreciated findings in contemporary SDT research. A dedicated focused analysis would examine: the specific instructional behaviors most associated with each form of need thwarting (autonomy thwarting via conditional regard and surveillance; competence thwarting via impossible standards and social comparison; relatedness thwarting via exclusion and indifference); the distinct psychological consequences of each form (controlled motivation, amotivation, ill-being, reactance); and the intervention implications that follow from treating thwarting as the primary target rather than satisfaction-maximization. Priority: **high** — the most direct extension of this analysis.

callouts.title: [[Autonomy-Support-in-Digital-and-AI-Mediated-Learning-Environments|Autonomy Support in Digital and AI-Mediated Learning Environments]]
callouts.body: The emergence of adaptive learning systems, AI tutors, gamified platforms, and learning analytics creates new terrain for SDT's principles. Does algorithmic personalization of challenge satisfy the competence need, or does it undermine autonomy by removing learner agency from challenge selection? Does learning analytics monitoring constitute surveillance (autonomy thwarting) or informational feedback (competence satisfying)? Does the absence of a teacher presence create a relatedness vacuum, or can virtual community features substitute? A focused analysis would examine how each of the three need mechanisms operates in digital environments, identify the specific design affordances and risks, and propose SDT-consistent design principles for technology-mediated learning. Priority: **high** — immediate practical relevance.

callouts.title: [[SDT and Formative Assessment: Feedback as Informational or Controlling]]
callouts.body: Assessment is the instructional domain where SDT's CET predictions are most directly actionable and most frequently violated. A focused analysis would examine: how rubric-based feedback, grade-first versus comment-first feedback delivery, peer assessment, portfolio assessment, and AI-generated feedback each affect the informational/controlling balance; what specific linguistic and structural features of feedback shift it toward the informational function; and how assessment frequency and stakes interact with CET predictions. The goal would be a SDT-consistent framework for feedback and assessment design grounded in the specific mechanisms identified in this analysis. Priority: **high**.

callouts.title: [[Cultural Universality vs. Cultural Moderation in SDT: A Critical Analysis]]
callouts.body: SDT's universality claim — that the three needs are universal in their importance — requires systematic empirical and theoretical scrutiny that a focused analysis would provide. This would examine: the evidence for and against universality from cross-cultural comparisons; the distinction between the universality of need importance and the cultural variability of what satisfies those needs; the collectivist-culture challenge to autonomy's primacy; and what genuine cultural sensitivity in SDT applications looks like (versus what counts as unjustified relativism). Priority: **high** — important for practitioners applying SDT in diverse contexts.

callouts.title: [[SDT Meets Achievement Goal Theory: Convergences, Divergences, and Integration Possibilities]]
callouts.body: SDT and Achievement Goal Theory (Elliot, Dweck) address overlapping motivational terrain: both predict that performance-approach and performance-avoidance goals are less educationally beneficial than mastery goals, and both ground these predictions in claims about cognitive processing. A focused analysis would map the conceptual overlap precisely, identify where the theories make different predictions (the role of competence feedback; the status of performance-approach goals), examine whether an integrated account is theoretically coherent, and consider what the integrated account would imply for instructional design. Priority: **medium** — high theoretical value, somewhat more specialized audience.

callouts.title: [[Internalization and Academic Identity: Why Some Students Never Reach Integrated Regulation]]
callouts.body: OIT predicts that under supportive conditions, learners will move toward identified and integrated regulation. Yet many students who have experienced reasonably supportive educational environments plateau at identified regulation — they value academic success instrumentally but have not integrated it with a genuine sense of academic identity. A focused analysis would examine: what distinguishes identified from integrated regulation in the academic domain; what conditions promote integration (not merely identification); the role of identity-relevant internalization versus value internalization; and how academic institutions can intentionally foster the integration of learning as a dimension of self. Priority: **medium** — especially relevant for higher education contexts.

wiki_links.section: Phase I: Orientation & Analytical Focus
wiki_links.context_line: [[Self-Determination-Theory|Self-Determination Theory]] (SDT), developed principally by [[Edward-Deci|Edward Deci]] and [[Richard-Ryan|Richard Ryan]] from the early 1970s onward, provides the most systematically developed and empirically tested account of *why* this happens — and, crucially, what conditions promote genuinely durable, deepening motivation. The theory's central architecture rests on three propositions: that human beings have evolved with inherent tendencies toward growth and integration; that this natural motivation depends on the satisfaction of three basic psychological needs (for [[Autonomy]], [[Competence]], and [[Relatedness]]); and that the social environment can either nurture or undermine this motivational substrate through the degree to which it supports or frustrates those needs.

wiki_links.section: Phase I: Orientation & Analytical Focus
wiki_links.context_line: For a comprehensive conceptual overview of SDT — its historical development, theoretical architecture, major sub-theories, and relationship to other motivational frameworks — see the [[Self-Determination-Theory-—-Foundational-Overview|Self-Determination Theory — Foundational Overview]]. This analysis presupposes familiarity with SDT's basic claims and focuses specifically on the learning context, the mechanisms of need satisfaction and thwarting, and the pedagogical implications that follow from a rigorous reading of the evidence.

wiki_links.section: Intrinsic Motivation and the Problem of Motivation's Origins
wiki_links.context_line: [[Intrinsic-Motivation|Intrinsic motivation]] is not, on SDT's account, a mysterious psychological force that some people possess and others lack. It is an evolved, baseline orientation of human beings toward exploration, mastery, and integration. Infants are not trained to be curious — curiosity is their default. The central theoretical question for SDT, therefore, is not how intrinsic motivation is created, but under what conditions it is *sustained* as development proceeds, or conversely, under what conditions it is undermined.

wiki_links.section: The Regulatory Spectrum: From Amotivation to Integration
wiki_links.context_line: One of SDT's most theoretically significant contributions is the recognition that not all extrinsic motivation is functionally equivalent. [[Organismic-Integration-Theory|Organismic Integration Theory]] (OIT), SDT's sub-theory governing extrinsic motivation, proposes that externally-originated behaviors can be progressively internalized and integrated, moving along a spectrum from completely external regulation to full integration.

wiki_links.section: The Evidence Landscape: Breadth, Depth, and Important Gaps
wiki_links.context_line: **Claim 2: Need thwarting produces consequences that differ in kind, not just degree, from need deprivation.** This is one of the most theoretically significant distinctions in recent SDT scholarship, and one the popular literature has been slow to absorb. [[Need-deprivation|Need deprivation]] refers to a passive absence of need satisfaction — a learning environment that provides no particular competence feedback, for example, neither satisfying nor actively frustrating competence. [[Need-Thwarting|Need thwarting]] refers to active frustration of a need — an environment that specifically undermines the student's sense of competence through criticism, comparison, or impossible standards.

wiki_links.context_line: **Claim 4: The competence need is particularly sensitive to feedback functional significance.** [[Cognitive-Evaluation-Theory|Cognitive Evaluation Theory]] (CET), SDT's sub-theory addressing the effects of external events on intrinsic motivation, proposes that all external events carry two aspects — an informational aspect (communicating something about competence) and a controlling aspect (communicating something about the locus of causality). When the informational aspect is salient, positive competence-relevant feedback enhances intrinsic motivation; when the controlling aspect is salient (feedback delivered as evaluation, comparison, or pressure), even positive feedback can undermine motivation.

wiki_links.section: The Mechanism of Competence: Optimal Challenge and the Informational Function
wiki_links.context_line: The competence mechanism operates through **effectance experience** — the moment-to-moment sense of being effective in interaction with the environment. This mechanism is tightly dependent on challenge calibration. [[Csikszentmihalyi]]'s [[Flow]] concept maps closely onto SDT's competence mechanism here: the optimal zone for competence experience — and for intrinsic motivation — is at the boundary where challenge slightly exceeds current skill, requiring effort and producing growth.

wiki_links.section: The Mechanism of Relatedness: Social Safety and the Risk Architecture of Learning
wiki_links.context_line: [[Conditional-Regard|Conditional regard]] — teacher warmth that is explicitly or implicitly contingent on academic performance — represents one of the most damaging forms of relatedness thwarting. Research by [[Avi-Assor|Avi Assor]] and colleagues shows that students who experience conditional regard from parents and teachers tend to develop **introjected regulation** rather than identified or integrated regulation: they internalize the contingency ("I am valuable when I succeed, worthless when I fail") rather than internalizing the value of learning itself. These students may perform at high levels under pressure but show elevated anxiety, fragile self-esteem, and collapse of motivation when success is not guaranteed. The paradox is that conditional regard appears, from the outside, to be supportive — the teacher cares about performance, after all. It is the contingency that is corrosive, not the caring.

SRL without SDT-compatible environments produces self-regulation in service of controlled goals.

wiki_links.section: Phase VII: PKB Connections & Cross-Report Links
wiki_links.context_line: > - **[[Psychological-Safety-in-Learning-Environments|Psychological Safety in Learning Environments]]** — Edmondson's psychological safety construct (developed in organizational contexts) maps directly onto SDT's relatedness mechanism and risk architecture analysis. Both frameworks converge on the same functional claim: when felt relational safety is absent, risk-taking (intellectual, creative, experimental) is suppressed. Cross-referencing these two literatures strengthens both: SDT provides the needs-based theoretical mechanism for why psychological safety matters, while the organizational literature provides implementation-level evidence about how team leaders and teachers can create safety through specific behaviors (listening, non-judgment, welcoming error as information).

wiki_links.section: Phase VII: PKB Connections & Cross-Report Links
wiki_links.context_line: > - **[[Expectancy-Value-Theory|Expectancy-Value Theory]]** — Wigfield and Eccles' expectancy-value theory addresses motivation through learners' expectations of success and subjective task value. SDT and EVT are complementary in identifying why task value matters: in SDT terms, perceiving a task as valuable is the cognitive marker of identified regulation — the student has cognitively connected the task to their own goals and values. SDT goes further by identifying the *environmental conditions* that promote this value integration (autonomy support, rationale provision), while EVT goes further in specifying the content of subjective value (utility, interest, attainment, cost). Together they provide a fuller picture of academic motivation than either alone.

wiki_links.section: Phase VII: PKB Connections & Cross-Report Links
wiki_links.context_line: > - **[[Gamification-in-Learning|Gamification in Learning]]** — Gamification is a theoretically interesting application domain for SDT because game mechanics can easily thwart or satisfy the three needs depending on implementation. Points, leaderboards, and badges are classic reward structures that CET predicts will undermine intrinsic motivation when they shift PLOC toward external — and the evidence from gamification research is consistent with this: competition-based leaderboards tend to undermine motivation for below-average performers and produce performance-goal orientation for all. Game mechanics that satisfy the competence need (optimal challenge, immediate feedback, mastery-based progression) and the autonomy need (choice, meaningful decisions, narrative agency) are more consistent with SDT's predictions about long-term engagement. This tension between popular gamification practice and SDT principles is a productive site for both research and design innovation.

wiki_links.section: Phase VII: PKB Connections & Cross-Report Links
wiki_links.context_line: > - **[[Self-Determination-Theory-—-Foundational-Overview|Self-Determination Theory — Foundational Overview]]** — This analysis extends the foundational treatment by drilling into the specific mechanisms through which each need drives learning outcomes, adding the need thwarting / need satisfaction asymmetry analysis, and offering the gateway model as an original synthesis. Readers should consult the foundational report for historical development, sub-theory architecture, and broad empirical landscape before engaging with this analysis.
